title: Erdoğan Signals Wider Nuclear Deal With Putin as Akkuyu Nears Commissioning; Ankara Pitches 'Electric TANAP' Green Grid
subhead: Turkey's first Russian-built nuclear plant is close to going live and Erdoğan has floated expanding nuclear cooperation with Moscow, while Ankara pushes a new green-electricity corridor with Azerbaijan, Georgia and Bulgaria — signaling energy diversification even as it deepens ties with the West.

sections.heading: Nuclear Ties With Russia Deepen as Akkuyu Nears Go-Live
sections.body:
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan told Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of a regional leaders' gathering in Kyrgyzstan that Russia and Turkey 'will take steps together to open some new power plants, along with the opening of the Akkuyu nuclear power plant,' according to RFI. The Akkuyu plant, built by Russia's Rosatom on Turkey's Mediterranean coast, is due online later this year, and Rosatom general manager Aleksey Likhachev said the first unit is 'just one step away from commissioning,' per Pravda Turkey.

Once operational, Akkuyu will supply up to 10 percent of Turkey's electricity. Rosatom owns the plant and will recoup its estimated €21.5 billion build cost by selling power, generating annual income of roughly €2-3 billion — a channel RFI notes Moscow could use to store liquidity in Turkish banks as Western sanctions tighten.
sections.whyItMatters: The deepening nuclear link cuts against the narrative of Turkey tilting fully toward Washington. As German Marshall Fund's Ozgur Unluhisarcikli put it to RFI, this is a 'gesture' to Putin consistent with Turkey's long-standing balancing act — Ankara competes with Russia regionally but won't sever the relationship.

sections.heading: Ankara Pitches 'Electric TANAP' Green Power Corridor
sections.body:
Turkish Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar said Ankara expects to sign an agreement with Azerbaijan, Georgia and Bulgaria at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya in November to build the 'Green Electricity Transmission and Trade' project — dubbed 'Electric TANAP' as a renewable-power echo of the existing gas pipeline, according to Pravda Turkey. The scheme positions Azerbaijan as the renewable source, Georgia as transit, Turkey as energy hub and Bulgaria as the EU entry point.

The plan builds on a 2025 memorandum providing for investment and integration with the ENTSO-E European system, and could later connect with Central Asia via the Middle Corridor.
sections.whyItMatters: It is Ankara's clearest bid yet to convert its gas-transit clout into a broader electricity role, and to bind the EU market into Caucasus-Turkey power flows — a hedge that runs parallel to, not instead of, deeper ties with Russia and the Gulf.

sections.heading: Foreign Policy: Fidan Calls for Hormuz Reopening, Blast Escalation in Gulf
sections.body:
Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, speaking at a joint press conference with his Azerbaijani counterpart in Baku, said reciprocal attacks in the Gulf are harming peace efforts to end the US-Iran war and called for them to stop immediately, adding that freedom of passage should be restored in the Strait of Hormuz and the pre-war status quo reinstated, per Reuters/JPost. Ankara says it is in touch with all parties.

The call came as Iran claimed an oil tanker exploded after hitting mines in Hormuz, while US Central Command rejected that account, saying the Panama-flagged El Gaia had been struck by an Iranian missile last month and again by an Iranian drone recently.
sections.whyItMatters: Turkey has direct skin in Hormuz — it imports Gulf crude — so Fidan's mediation pitch pairs Ankara's economic interest with a diplomatic role straddling both the US and Iran, consistent with its energy-driven balancing abroad.

sections.heading: Economy & Energy: Black Sea Drilling and $200B Grid Plan
sections.body: Turkey is expanding its Black Sea energy push with new oil drilling while building out supporting infrastructure, including LNG regasification capacity it aims to raise to 200 million cubic metres per day plus pipeline links with neighbours, according to Bytes Europe. Separately, Turkey plans roughly $200 billion in energy investment by 2035 to expand renewables, develop nuclear power and modernise the electricity grid, per a 2026 Energy Sector Report prepared by the Presidential Investment and Finance Office cited by Megaproject.
sections.whyItMatters: The figures show the scale of Ankara's bet on energy self-sufficiency — domestic Black Sea gas/oil, LNG import flexibility and a nuclear baseline — a strategy that both lowers its import bill and reinforces Moscow as a key supplier.

sections.heading: Syria Update: SDF Integration and Erdoğan's Coming Visit
sections.body: Foreign Minister Fidan said in Damascus that the integration of all armed groups under Syria's central state is 'essential' for sovereignty and territorial integrity, and welcomed the SDF's steps toward dissolving into state institutions as an 'important initiative' that must now be implemented 'without wasting time,' per Anadolu Agency/anews. Fidan confirmed Erdoğan is planning a visit to Syria in the near future and said officials are preparing. Turkey and Syria have signed some 40 agreements and memoranda of understanding linking 22 Syrian ministries to Turkish counterparts, SANA reported via the Jerusalem Post.
sections.whyItMatters: No major new step today beyond what Ankara has already signalled, but the Damascus track is moving — and the pace of integration plus Erdoğan's planned visit is drawing growing wariness from Israel, with JISS President Efraim Inbar telling the Jerusalem Post that Turkish influence and forces in Syria pose a risk to Israel.

sections.heading: Domestic: Izmir Raids Keep LGBTQ Crackdown in Spotlight
sections.body: Turkey jailed 16 people after raids on LGBTQ+ groups in Izmir, with the Turkish Human Rights Association describing the operation as 'state-led discrimination, politics of fear and the dismantling of civil society,' per Reuters/JPost. In a separate operation, at least 26 people were detained in raids targeting LGBTQ+ associations over accusations of obscenity.
sections.whyItMatters: The widening crackdown continues to draw EU criticism and pressure — a recurring friction point between Ankara and Brussels even as political and defense ties improve.

bottomLine: The day's strongest signal is energy. Erdoğan is pairing the imminent commissioning of Russia-built Akkuyu with an offer of even wider nuclear cooperation with Moscow, even as Ankara pushes a parallel green-electricity corridor toward the EU and expands Black Sea and LNG capacity. That dual-track approach — more Russian nuclear and more European grid integration at once — is Turkey's signature balancing act in action: extract what it needs from every bloc without committing to any. Foreign policy stayed active with Fidan's Hormuz mediation push, while the Syria integration file and the LGBTQ crackdown hold steady without qualitative change. Expect the Akkuyu go-live and Erdoğan's Syria visit to be the next landmarks.
sources: RFI, Pravda Turkey, Reuters via Jerusalem Post, Anadolu Agency/anews, Jerusalem Post (Seth Frantzman/Danielle Greyman-Kennard), Bytes Europe, Megaproject
